position: Refactor in place this year, but spend a small fixed slice of that work on profiling and on making the storage format explicitly reversible, so that a streaming rebuild in a later year does not require a second migration.

claims.text: Before either path is chosen, the pipeline must be profiled, because the entire question turns on whether the slowness is a handful of local hotspots or a genuine architectural ceiling, and neither recommendation is defensible without that data.

If profiling shows hotspots, refactoring wins on cost; if it shows the batch window colliding with the next run or per-batch overhead dominating at scale, refactoring cannot help and the rebuild becomes necessary regardless of slack.

The rebuild's distinctive risk is not that it discards tacit correctness handling — refactoring the same code paths risks that too — but that a one-way door on storage format taken under zero slack removes the retreat path precisely when the schedule is most likely to force a half-finished migration.

Storage format and processing paradigm are coupled at the data-model level — batch favors time-partitioned immutable segments, streaming favors key-partitioned stateful layouts — so the honest move is not to claim decoupling is cheap but to pick a format whose migration cost is bounded and known, and to write that cost down now.

Deferring the rebuild is only sound if a specific future year is expected to have slack; if no year will, the choice is not refactor-versus-rebuild but rebuild-under-pressure-now versus rebuild-under-pressure-later on a more degraded system, and later is worse.

assumptions: The performance problem has not been rigorously profiled yet; if it has, the profile should replace claims 1 and 2 outright and may well favor the rebuild.
"No slack" is a real constraint this year, but I no longer assume it is unique to this year — if it is structural, my recommendation weakens substantially.
Business requirements do not include a committed sub-minute freshness SLA that batch cannot meet at any refactoring effort.
The team has not already run a streaming system in production; if they have, my risk estimate for the rebuild is meaningfully too high.
Streaming may improve throughput and cost as well as latency, via incremental reprocessing instead of full reruns, so the rebuild's upside is larger than a pure latency framing suggests.
would_change_my_mind: Profiling shows time spread thinly across the pipeline with no hotspot above roughly 15 percent of runtime, indicating a structural rather than local problem.
Growth projections show the batch window colliding with the next batch's start inside 12–18 months, making the current design terminal rather than merely inefficient.
A committed product requirement exists for sub-minute or continuous freshness with a date attached, which refactoring cannot reach.
The last three years show no year with meaningful slack and none projected, which converts "defer the rebuild" into "never rebuild" and inverts my recommendation.
A credible migration estimate shows moving between batch-optimized and stream-optimized storage later costs comparably to doing it now, in which case the sequencing argument loses its force.
Leadership will actually grant slack — named features cut from the roadmap in writing — which would remove my central objection to rebuilding this year.
nuance: The hidden failure mode is not choosing wrong, it is choosing the rebuild and stalling at 70 percent for eighteen months running two pipelines and reconciling them — but the mirror failure, deferring forever because no year ever has slack, ends in the same place more slowly.
